{{Short description|Generalization of the ellipse to allow more than two foci}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''n''-ellipse}}
[[File:N-ellipse.svg|thumb|right|300px|Examples of 3-ellipses for three given foci. The progression of the distances is not linear.]]

In [[geometry]], the '''{{mvar|n}}-ellipse''' is a [[generalization]] of the [[ellipse]] allowing more than two [[focus (geometry)|foci]].<ref name=Sekino/>  {{mvar|n}}-ellipses go by numerous other names, including '''multifocal ellipse''',<ref name=erdos/> '''polyellipse''',<ref name=Melzak/> '''egglipse''',<ref name=Sahadevan/>  '''{{mvar|k}}-ellipse''',<ref name=NPS/> and '''Tschirnhaus'sche Eikurve''' (after [[Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus]]).  They were first investigated by [[James Clerk Maxwell]] in 1846.<ref name=Maxwell/>

Given {{mvar|n}} focal points {{math|(''u''<sub>''i''</sub>,&thinsp;''v''<sub>''i''</sub>)}} in a plane, an {{mvar|n}}-ellipse is the [[locus (mathematics)|locus]] of points of the plane whose sum of distances to the {{mvar|n}} foci is a constant {{mvar|d}}. In formulas, this is the set

: <math>\left\{(x, y) \in \mathbf{R}^2: \sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{(x-u_i)^2 + (y-v_i)^2} = d\right\}.</math>

The 1-ellipse is the [[circle]], and the 2-ellipse is the classic ellipse. Both are [[algebraic curve]]s of degree&nbsp;2.

For any number {{mvar|n}} of foci, the {{mvar|n}}-ellipse is a [[closed curve|closed]], [[convex curve]].<ref name=erdos>{{cite journal|first1=Paul|last1=Erdős|author-link1=Paul Erdős|first2=István|last2=Vincze|author-link2=István Vincze (mathematician)|title=On the Approximation of Convex, Closed Plane Curves by Multifocal Ellipses|journal=Journal of Applied Probability|date=1982|volume=19|pages=89–96|jstor=3213552|url=http://renyi.mta.hu/~p_erdos/1982-18.pdf|accessdate=22 February 2015|doi=10.2307/3213552|s2cid=17166889 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160928200222/http://renyi.mta.hu/~p_erdos/1982-18.pdf|archive-date=28 September 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>{{rp|(p. 90)}} The curve is [[smoothness|smooth]] unless it goes through a focus.<ref name=NPS/>{{rp|p.7}} 

The ''n''-ellipse is in general a subset of the points satisfying a particular [[algebraic equation]].<ref name=NPS/>{{rp|Figs. 2 and 4; p. 7}} If ''n'' is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]], the algebraic degree of the curve is <math>2^n</math>, while if ''n'' is [[parity (mathematics)|even]] the degree is <math>2^n - \binom{n}{n/2}.</math><ref name=NPS>J. Nie, P.A. Parrilo, B. Sturmfels: "[http://math.ucsd.edu/~njw/PUBLICPAPERS/kellipse_imaproc_toappear.pdf J. Nie, P. Parrilo, B.St.: "Semidefinite representation of the k-ellipse", in ''Algorithms in Algebraic Geometry'', I.M.A. Volumes in Mathematics and its Applications, 146, Springer, New York, 2008, pp. 117-132]</ref>{{rp|(Thm. 1.1)}}

''n''-ellipses are special cases of [[Spectrahedron|spectrahedra]].
